items.title: U.S. Treasury Yields Fall Ahead of PCE Inflation Data - MarketWatch
items.excerpt: U.S. Treasury yields fell in Asian trading on Wednesday as investors awaited October personal consumption expenditures inflation data and the second estimate of third-quarter gross domestic product. The two-year Treasury yield declined 4.4 basis points to 4.626%, while the 10-year yield fell 3.6 basis points to 4.864%, according to Tradeweb. The PCE price index--the Federal Reserve's favored gauge of inflation--"carries extra weight this month," said Natalia Lojevsky, managing director and head of wealth solutions at CIFC Asset Management. "Markets already expect a December hike so an in-line or hot print mostly keeps that on track," she said. "The bigger signal to watch is how long the Fed stays in tightening mode into 2027. One soft print likely won't change the current track, it would take a run of them." Analysts polled by The Wall Street Journal expect headline PCE inflation to have accelerated to 3.8% on the year in October, up from 3.6% in September. Core PCE, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, is forecast to have risen to 3.2% from 3.1%. "Wednesday's core PCE should be a worry for Treasurys, as a rise to 3.2% year-on-year is the central market expectation," ING rates strategists Padhraic Garvey and Benjamin Schroeder said in a note. While lower energy prices should help tame headline inflation ahead, that does little for core inflation rates, or, at the very least, it will take a bit longer to feed through, they added.

items.title: Alaska ends deal to give voter records to US Justice Department | US Midterm Elections 2026 News | Al Jazeera
items.excerpt: Published On 25 Nov 2026 25 Nov 2026 Alaska has terminated a memorandum of understanding that granted the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) access to the state’s voter rolls. On Monday, outgoing Lieutenant Governor Nancy Dahlstrom, who oversees the state’s elections, announced she had notified the Justice Department that Alaska was withdrawing from the 2025 memo, effective immediately. In a statement, Dahlstrom said her state had entered the agreement “in good faith to cooperate with our federal law enforcement partners”. But she acknowledged a shift had taken place after the 2026 midterm elections. “The circumstances have now changed,” Dahlstrom wrote. “The election has concluded and the agreement no longer serves a continuing purpose.” The reversal comes after months of pressure from the administration of President Donald Trump for states to surrender their voter rolls to federal authorities. Trump has argued that such information was necessary to root out fraud during the November 3 midterms. But officials in certain states argued that the federal government was encroaching on their constitutional authority. Under the US Constitution, only states have the power to administer elections. Experts have also called Trump’s claims of “rigged” elections unsubstantiated. ## No voters flagged for removal The memorandum, signed last December at the Justice Department’s behest, established terms under which federal officials could flag potentially ineligible voters on Alaska’s voter rolls. “Since that time, the DOJ has not identiﬁed any potentially ineligible voters or raised concerns regarding Alaska’s voter registration records,” the state Division of Elections said. “No voters were removed from Alaska’s voter rolls as a result of the agreement.” ... His administration sued some 30 ... Twenty-eight of those cases were ultimately dismissed in court, according to the Brennan Center for Justice, a public policy institute at New York University. The Justice Department suffered a further setback last month when a federal judge struck down its nationwide voter-list maintenance programme, ruling that it lacked legal authority to collect and assess state registration lists. The administration has appealed the ruling. Alaska was one of at least 16 states that complied with the administration’s demands for voter roll access. But it was sued by voting rights advocates for surrendering voter information, in violation of the Alaska Constitution.

items.title: Poll finds US voters want government to end Iran war regardless of terms | US-Israel war on Iran News | Al Jazeera
items.excerpt: A new poll has found that a majority of voters in the United States want an end to the US-Israel war on Iran immediately, even if it means accepting less favourable conditions. Overall, 55 percent of those surveyed agreed with an “end to the war now, regardless of the terms”. That number was even higher among Democrats and independents, who agreed with the statement at a rate of 80 percent and 59 percent, respectively. About 25 percent of Republicans said the same. A majority of Democratic voters also supported steps to pressure the administration of President Donald Trump to stop the conflict. Fifty-three percent of party members said they would favour Congress withholding funding for military operations, and 51 percent would back an “an Iran war-funding cutoff” in upcoming budget negotiations, even if the manoeuvre risked a government shutdown. The numbers were published on Tuesday as part of the latest Critical Issues Poll, released by the University of Maryland and the research firm Ipsos. Shibley Telhami, the poll’s principal investigator, said he was surprised by the level of support for ending the war, regardless of the terms. “We knew that people were strongly opposed to this war and wanted it to end,” he told Al Jazeera in a phone call. “What we were less sure of is what they would be willing to accept to achieve this.” The survey asked 1,022 US adults about their perspectives on the war. In one question, they were tasked with assessing with three options: whether to end the conflict immediately, escalate militarily, or continue on the current path in order to extract concessions from Iran. Just 21 percent of all respondents favoured the current path, and 18 percent supported escalation. “Clearly, the public mood is to end it now, whatever it takes,” said Telhami. ... Voters also appear sceptical about the US government’s arguments in favour of the war, which include dismantling Iran’s nuclear programme. The Critical Issues Poll found that only 28 percent of those surveyed believed that the war had left Iran in “worse position” to develop nuclear weapons. While the US has long voiced concerned that Iran could pursue nuclear arms, intelligence assessments have not found evidence that Tehran has authorised such a step since abandoning its nuclear weapons programme in 2003.

items.title: Miley Cyrus wedding guest responds after sparking outrage with wardrobe faux pas | The Independent
items.excerpt: Wednesday 25 November 2026 03:14 EST ... When a guest at Miley Cyrus’s wedding broke the dress code by wearing a yellow gown, the internet dubbed her “rude” and “embarrassing” – but the bride herself apparently wasn’t so bothered. The “Flowers” singer, 33, married musician Maxx Morando, 28, in an intimate backyard ceremony in Palm Springs on Saturday (21 November). The pair have been together for five years, with Morando proposing to Cyrus during a holiday to Japan in 2025. After photos of the occasion emerged, however, one guest went viral for the wrong reasons – appearing to break the all-black dress code by wearing a mustard yellow dress. The guest has since been identified as Belgica Vargas, who attended the wedding alongside her husband, the music producer Shawn Everett, who has worked with Cyrus. An aerial photograph of the wedding ceremony, in which Vargas’s yellow gown stands out amid a sea of black and dark tones, has been widely circulated on social media, where it has accumulated over 40 million views. Backlash quickly followed, with fans describing Vargas as “embarrassing” and “rude” over the obvious wardrobe faux-pas. But according to Vargas’s sister, Grecia, Cyrus was not at all concerned by the dress code violation, which was the result of Vargas misreading the invitation. “[Belgica] didn’t know guys, her husband is really good friends with Miley and if you knew my bro in law then you would totally understand,” Grecia wrote in a comment that has received over 8,000 likes at the time of writing. “My sister should have known better to double check on the invite,” she continued.
